records.name: Calvert family (Lords Baltimore; Calverts of Mount Airy and Riversdale)
records.scaleNote: As Maryland's proprietors they presided over the 1664 law making slavery lifelong and hereditary; their Riversdale descendants enslaved c. 15–32 people (1800–1806 tax lists) and Charles Benedict Calvert held 52 people in 1860, per UMD's 1856 Project.
records.base: St. Mary's City and Riversdale (Riverdale Park), Maryland
records.origins: George Calvert, 1st Baron Baltimore, sought a colonial charter; it was granted in 1632 to his son Cecil Calvert, 2nd Lord Baltimore, and Maryland was settled from 1634 as a proprietary colony. The family held proprietary power (with interruptions) until the Revolution, and an American branch descended from Benedict Swingate Calvert, son of the 5th Lord Baltimore, settled at Mount Airy (Prince George's County).
records.role_summary: Under the proprietorship, Maryland's assembly in 1664 — with Charles Calvert (later 3rd Lord Baltimore) as governor — enacted that enslaved Africans would serve 'durante vita' (for life), a foundation of Maryland's tobacco slave economy. Later Calverts were themselves planters: George Calvert (1768–1838) and Rosalie Stier Calvert ran Riversdale with enslaved labor, and their son Charles Benedict Calvert enslaved 52 people in 1860.

roleDetail.d: The 1664 Maryland act, passed under the proprietary government, made the status of enslaved Africans lifelong and extended it to their children, per the Maryland State Archives.
Tax assessments record c. 15 enslaved people at Riversdale in 1800 and 32 in 1806; diarist Adam Francis Plummer was enslaved there by George Calvert and then Charles Benedict Calvert.

roleDetail.t: Founding a university with plantation wealth.
roleDetail.d: Charles Benedict Calvert donated land from Riversdale for the Maryland Agricultural College (1856), now the University of Maryland, College Park; he held 52 people in slavery in 1860, per the 1856 Project.

roleDetail.t: Family ties across the Chesapeake gentry.
roleDetail.d: Eleanor Calvert, George Calvert's sister, married John Parke Custis (Martha Washington's son) in 1774, linking the Calverts to Mount Vernon.

records.legacy: Calvert County and the city of Baltimore carry the family's name and title. Riversdale is now a house museum run by M-NCPPC that interprets its enslaved workforce and seeks descendants of the people enslaved there; the University of Maryland's 1856 Project (2024 report) documents Calvert's role in its founding.

legacyDetail.d: The museum researches and presents the enslaved community at Riversdale and is actively seeking their descendants.
The university's 2024 report 'Reconstructing the Truth' estimates more than 500 enslaved people lived on land that became the college.

sources.label: Maryland State Archives — Blacks Before the Law in Colonial Maryland
UMD Libraries — The 1856 Project releases inaugural research report

records.today: The Barons Baltimore title died out in 1771, and the proprietary estates were confiscated in the Revolution. The Maryland Calverts' houses are public: Riversdale (M-NCPPC) and Mount Airy (Rosaryville State Park). The University of Maryland's 1856 Project studies the enslaved people who built Charles Benedict Calvert's fortune, and Riversdale has sought descendants of the people enslaved there. No living Calvert descendants are named here.

records.name: Macon family (Gideon Macon of Virginia; Nathaniel Macon of North Carolina)
records.scaleNote: Nathaniel Macon's father left 3,000 acres and 25–30 enslaved people in 1761; Nathaniel held dozens at Buck Spring (c. 70 by some accounts). The family's weight lies in politics: Nathaniel was Speaker of the U.S. House 1801–1807 and a leading defender of slavery.
records.base: Buck Spring, Warren County, North Carolina
records.origins: Gideon Macon (d. 1702), a New Kent County, Virginia planter and member of the House of Burgesses (1696), founded the Virginia line; through his daughter Martha he was great-grandfather of Martha Dandridge Custis Washington. A branch moved to North Carolina, where Maj. Gideon Macon left his son Nathaniel (1757/58–1837) three enslaved people, George, Robb and Lucy, in 1761.
records.role_summary: Nathaniel Macon farmed tobacco and grain at Buck Spring with enslaved labor while serving 37 years in Congress (Speaker 1801–1807, then Senator). NCpedia describes him as a staunch advocate of states' rights and of slavery; he opposed congressional restriction of slavery in the Missouri debates of 1819–1821.

roleDetail.d: His father's 1761 estate included 3,000 acres and 25–30 enslaved people; three were bequeathed to Nathaniel.
Macon was Speaker of the House (1801–1807) when Congress passed the 1807 Act Prohibiting Importation of Slaves — a ban that left the domestic trade intact.
He opposed the Missouri Compromise as conceding too much power to Congress over slavery, per NCpedia and Encyclopedia.com.

records.legacy: Macon, Georgia; Fort Macon; Macon County (NC and elsewhere); and Randolph-Macon College (chartered 1830, named for Macon and John Randolph) honor him. Buck Spring is on the National Register of Historic Places (1970); its interpretation of the enslaved community has been limited.

legacyDetail.d: A city, a fort, several counties and a Virginia college bear the Macon name.
Nathaniel Macon was a second cousin of Martha Washington through the Virginia Macons.

connections.label: Gideon Macon was Martha Washington's great-grandfather

lineage.name: Gideon Macon
lineage.note: New Kent County, Virginia planter and burgess; founder of the Virginia line.

lineage.name: Martha Macon Jones
lineage.note: Married Orlando Jones; their daughter Frances Jones married John Dandridge.

lineage.name: Martha Dandridge Custis Washington
lineage.note: Gideon Macon's great-granddaughter; the Custis dower estate she brought to George Washington was built on enslaved labor.

lineage.name: Maj. Gideon Macon (North Carolina)
lineage.note: Left his son Nathaniel three enslaved people, George, Robb and Lucy.

lineage.name: Nathaniel Macon
lineage.note: Speaker of the U.S. House (1801–1807) and senator, a firm defender of slavery, who enslaved dozens of people at Buck Spring.

lineage.name: Hannah Plummer Macon

lineage.name: Daughters' families

records.today: No publicly documented descendants have been traced. The family's main legacy is its name, on Macon (Georgia), Fort Macon, several Macon counties and Randolph-Macon College; Buck Spring survives as a historic site.

records.name: Contee family of Prince George's County
records.scaleNote: A Prince George's/Anne Arundel tobacco-planting and mercantile family. Formerly enslaved Dennis Simms (b. 1841) recalled more than 100 enslaved people on the Contee plantation of Richard and Charles Contee (WPA interview, 1937), and Prince George's Slave Statistics (1868–69) record people declared by the administrator of John Contee's estate (per Maryland State Archives). No full count of family holdings has been published.
records.base: Nottingham and 'Contee', Prince George's County, Maryland
records.origins: Col. Thomas Contee lived at 'Brookefield' (now 'The Valley') near Nottingham on the Patuxent; his son Benjamin Contee (1755–1815), a Revolutionary officer, sat in the Confederation Congress and the first U.S. House (1789–1791), and with his brother Alexander ran stores at Nottingham, Queen Anne and Upper Marlboro. Through marriage, Capt. John Contee acquired the Snowden plantation Oaklands near Laurel.
records.role_summary: The Contees were part of southern Maryland's tobacco gentry, whose wealth rested on enslaved labor. Dennis Simms, interviewed by the Federal Writers' Project in 1937, described being enslaved on a Contee tobacco plantation (identified by the Smithsonian as Java Farm, next to Woodlawn), with frequent whippings, bans on reading and church, and secret gatherings for spirituals.

roleDetail.d: Simms's testimony describes over 100 enslaved workers on the Contee estate in the 1840s–1850s; it is a single late recollection and should be read as testimony.

Maryland State Archives' index to Prince George's freedom records lists people (e.g. Annetta Contee, 25; Walter Contee, 2) declared in the 1868–69 Slave Statistics by Daniel Clarke, administrator of John Contee's estate.
The Contee brothers' Patuxent stores linked them to the tobacco export economy that ran through Chesapeake river ports.
Oaklands (also called 'Contee'), a Snowden slave plantation that passed to Capt. John Contee by marriage, had overseers remembered as especially cruel in the mid-1800s.

records.legacy: The Prince George's County locality of Contee (near Laurel) and Contee Road preserve the name. Descendants of people enslaved on Contee land appear in Maryland's freedom records and 1867–68 slave statistics, and the Smithsonian's Woodlawn History Center (opened 2022) interprets Simms's testimony with local descendants.

legacyDetail.d: Smithsonian Environmental Research Center exhibits draw on Simms's oral history of Java Farm.
Many free and enslaved people recorded as 'Contee' appear in county records; the surname alone does not establish who enslaved them.

lineage.note: Prince George's County planter and merchant; father of Jane Contee Hanson.

lineage.name: Jane Contee Hanson
lineage.note: Married John Hanson (President of Congress under the Articles, 1781–82), himself an enslaver; their marriage linked the two families' estates.

lineage.note: Planter at Brookefield near Nottingham on the Patuxent.

lineage.name: Benjamin Contee
lineage.note: Revolutionary officer, Confederation Congress delegate and first-Congress representative; later an Episcopal clergyman; ran stores with his brother Alexander.

lineage.name: Capt. John Contee

records.today: No publicly documented descendants have been traced; the Contee estates were broken up after emancipation in 1864. The name survives in the Contee area near Laurel and Contee Road, and the related Hanson line in John Hanson's statue in the U.S. Capitol.

records.name: George Washington
records.scaleNote: Mount Vernon's June 1799 census lists 317 enslaved people on five farms: 123 owned by Washington, 153 Custis 'dower' people, and c. 40 rented from a neighbor, per Mount Vernon.
records.origins: Washington inherited ten enslaved people at age eleven on his father's death in 1743, and later Mount Vernon from his half-brother Lawrence's estate. His 1759 marriage to the widow Martha Dandridge Custis brought control of the Custis 'dower' enslaved people.
records.role_summary: Washington built Mount Vernon (8,000 acres) into a tobacco, then wheat, milling, fishing and distilling enterprise worked by enslaved people. He bought and occasionally sold people — in 1766 he shipped Tom, a foreman he called a 'Rogue & Runaway', to St. Kitts in exchange for rum, molasses and other goods — and as president signed the 1793 Fugitive Slave Act.

roleDetail.d: Washington's own census recorded every enslaved person at Mount Vernon by farm, family and task.
Washington sold Tom to the West Indies in 1766 and at least two other people to the Caribbean as punishment, per Mount Vernon.

His will freed the 123 people he owned after Martha's death (they were freed 1 January 1801); William Lee was freed outright. The 153 dower people could not be freed by him and passed to Custis heirs, splitting families.

records.legacy: Mount Vernon, owned by the Mount Vernon Ladies' Association since 1858, now interprets slavery extensively, with a Slave Memorial (1983, designed by Howard University students) and archaeology of the enslaved burial ground. The capital, a state, and countless institutions bear his name.

legacyDetail.d: Archaeology since 2014 has mapped graves at Mount Vernon's enslaved cemetery.
Mount Vernon's digital encyclopedia profiles individuals such as William Lee, Ona Judge and Tom, drawing on Washington's own records.

lineage.note: Built Mount Vernon and married into the Fairfax family; George leased Mount Vernon from Lawrence's widow from 1754 and inherited it in 1761.

lineage.name: Martha Dandridge Custis Washington
lineage.note: The 1759 marriage gave Washington control of the Custis dower lands and enslaved people.

lineage.name: William Lee
lineage.note: Washington's enslaved valet through the Revolution; the only person freed outright by his 1799 will.

lineage.name: John Parke Custis and Eleanor Calvert
lineage.note: Their children were raised at Mount Vernon and inherited Custis people.

lineage.name: Bushrod Washington
lineage.note: Supreme Court justice who inherited Mount Vernon in 1802 and sold 54 enslaved people to Louisiana for $10,000 in 1821.

lineage.name: John Augustine Washington III
lineage.note: Last private owner; sold Mount Vernon to the Mount Vernon Ladies' Association in 1858.

records.today: Washington had no biological children, so there are no direct descendants; collateral Washington and Custis lines are numerous but private and not named here. Martha freed his 123 enslaved people in 1801, while the Custis dower people passed to her grandchildren. Mount Vernon, owned by the Mount Vernon Ladies' Association since 1858, works with descendants of the enslaved community.

records.name: Custis family (Martha Washington's Custis estate; Arlington)
records.scaleNote: 153 Custis 'dower' people lived at Mount Vernon in 1799; George Washington Parke Custis later owned nearly 200 people, as many as 63 at Arlington, per NPS.
records.base: Arlington House, Arlington, Virginia (also White House and Romancoke on the Pamunkey)
records.origins: Daniel Parke Custis, a wealthy Tidewater planter, died in 1757 leaving a large estate of land and enslaved people; his widow Martha's dower share went with her into her marriage to George Washington. Their grandson George Washington Parke Custis (1781–1857) inherited Custis people and built Arlington House from 1802.
records.role_summary: The Custis estate supplied much of Mount Vernon's enslaved workforce; on Martha Washington's death (1802) the dower people were divided among her grandchildren. G.W.P. Custis brought enslaved people, most born at Mount Vernon, to Arlington in 1802; his 1857 will required their freedom within five years, and his son-in-law Robert E. Lee kept them working to settle debts until filing a deed of manumission in late 1862.

roleDetail.d: Because dower people belonged to the Custis estate, Washington could not free them; in 1802 they were split among Custis heirs.
Custis owned nearly 200 people across Arlington, White House and Romancoke; NPS interprets the Syphax, Burke, Parks and Gray families.
John Parke Custis married Eleanor Calvert (1774), and Mary Custis married Robert E. Lee (1831).

records.legacy: Arlington House (NPS) now sits within Arlington National Cemetery, and the park has expanded its interpretation of the enslaved community, including restoring the slave quarters. Descendants of the Syphax family, enslaved by Custis, became prominent in Washington, D.C.

legacyDetail.d: NPS presents enslaved residents' stories and has sought to change the memorial's naming so it does not center Lee.
After federal seizure, Arlington land hosted Freedman's Village (1863) for formerly enslaved people.

sources.label: Mount Vernon — The Growth of Mount Vernon's Enslaved Community
NPS — Robert E. Lee and Slavery

Private living descendants are not named.

records.name: Andrew Jackson
records.scaleNote: The Jackson family owned more than 300 people over the decades and about 150 at his death in 1845, per The Hermitage; he bought and sold people from 1788 to 1844, much of it in the Natchez and New Orleans markets.
records.origins: A lawyer and land speculator on the Tennessee frontier, Jackson bought his first enslaved person in 1788. In 1804 he moved to the Hermitage tract with nine enslaved people, and cotton planting there became the base of his wealth.
records.role_summary: Jackson was both a cotton planter and an active slave trader: he marketed coffles of enslaved people in the Natchez District, the Felicianas and New Orleans, writing in 1812 that his costs for 'Negroes sent to markett' rarely exceeded fifteen dollars a head. In 1811 he confronted federal Indian agent Silas Dinsmoor, who demanded passes for a coffle Jackson was driving south.

roleDetail.d: Cotton grown by enslaved people at the Hermitage made Jackson rich; roughly 150 people were enslaved there by 1845.
Historians document his buying and selling of people from 1788 to 1844, including speculative coffles sent down the Natchez Trace.
As president he backed suppression of abolitionist mailings (1835) and his Indian Removal policy opened Native lands to cotton slavery.

records.legacy: The Hermitage (Andrew Jackson Foundation) now presents the stories of the enslaved community and in December 2024 announced it had located the enslaved cemetery, with at least 28 burials; an advisory committee includes descendants. Jackson's place on the $20 bill and statues remain debated.

legacyDetail.d: Ground-penetrating radar and limited excavation confirmed the burial ground about 1,000 feet from the mansion.
The Hermitage is including descendants of the enslaved in planning interpretation of the site.

records.today: The Hermitage is run by the Andrew Jackson Foundation, which works with descendants of the enslaved community and in 2024 located its cemetery. Jackson had no biological children; Andrew Jackson Jr.'s descendants lived at the Hermitage into the late 19th century, and no living descendants are named here.

records.name: Johnson brothers of Maryland (Gov. Thomas Johnson; Catoctin Furnace)
records.scaleNote: Baker Johnson's 1809 will lists more than 80 enslaved people, many skilled ironworkers, at Catoctin Furnace, per Maryland DNR.
records.origins: Thomas Johnson (1732–1819), born in Calvert County, was a Frederick lawyer, Continental Congress delegate, Maryland's first elected governor (1777–1779) and briefly a U.S. Supreme Court justice (1791–1793). With his brothers James, Baker and Roger he founded the Catoctin ironworks in the 1770s.
records.role_summary: The Johnsons built Catoctin Furnace on the labor of enslaved African Americans, who worked as colliers, founders, forgemen, blacksmiths, farmhands and domestic servants; the furnace supplied iron during the Revolution. By mid-century hired immigrant labor replaced enslaved workers, and some enslaved workers may have been sold south.

roleDetail.d: Enslaved craftsmen held skilled posts at the furnace; named individuals in Baker Johnson's will include Collier Sam and the waggoners Henry and Harvey.
Thomas Johnson nominated Washington as commander-in-chief in 1775 and governed Maryland during the war while his family's furnace relied on enslaved labor.
As immigrant labor became cheaper, some enslaved Catoctin workers may have been sold to the Deep South.

records.legacy: The Catoctin Furnace African American Cemetery is thought to be the most complete Black cemetery tied to early American industry. A 2023 Science study (Smithsonian, Harvard, 23andMe, Catoctin Furnace Historical Society) sequenced 27 people buried there and linked nearly 42,000 living people to them; facial reconstructions were unveiled in 2021.

legacyDetail.d: The 2023 study identified five families among those buried and found the closest living relatives concentrated in Maryland.
The furnace stack and village lie in Cunningham Falls State Park, interpreted by the Historical Society.

lineage.note: Founded the Catoctin ironworks and owned it jointly, then divided their holdings in 1793.

lineage.name: Joshua Johnson

lineage.name: Ann Jennings Johnson

records.name: Andrew Johnson
records.scaleNote: A household enslaver, not a planter: bills of sale show he bought Sam (c. 13) for $541 in 1842 and Dolly (c. 19) for $500 in 1843; NPS says he owned at least ten people at most.
records.origins: A tailor from a poor North Carolina family, Johnson rose through Tennessee politics. As his fortunes grew he bought enslaved people for his Greeneville household.
records.role_summary: Johnson owned a small number of people — Dolly, her half-brother Sam, Dolly's children and others — and, per family tradition, freed them on 8 August 1863. As military governor of Tennessee he sought the state's exemption from the Emancipation Proclamation, and as president (1865–1869) he opposed Reconstruction measures protecting freedpeople.

roleDetail.d: NPS holds bills of sale for Sam (1842) and Dolly (1843).
8 August became Emancipation Day in East Tennessee; in 1871 Sam Johnson served as 'Officer of the Day' at Greeneville's celebration.
He vetoed the Freedmen's Bureau and Civil Rights bills of 1866; Congress overrode the latter.

records.legacy: The Andrew Johnson National Historic Site (NPS) in Greeneville interprets the people he enslaved, including Sam Johnson, who in 1867 obtained land from Johnson for a school for Black children. The question of Johnson's paternity of Dolly's children is unresolved.

legacyDetail.d: The park's 'Slaves of Andrew Johnson' history page names the enslaved household and its descendants.

sources.label: American Battlefield Trust — Andrew Johnson National Historic Site
Wikipedia — Andrew Johnson National Historic Site

lineage.name: Jacob Johnson
lineage.note: Raleigh porter who died when Andrew was three, leaving the family poor.

lineage.name: James Selby
lineage.note: Raleigh tailor to whom Andrew was bound at about age ten; Andrew and his brother William ran away after about five years and Selby advertised a reward.

lineage.name: Eliza McCardle Johnson
lineage.note: Married him in 1827 and helped him improve his reading and writing.

lineage.name: Dolly, Sam and Henry
lineage.note: Dolly was bought in 1843, then her half-brother Sam, and Henry in 1857; he held at least ten people and freed them on 8 August 1863.

lineage.name: Martha Johnson Patterson
lineage.note: White House hostess during his presidency.

lineage.name: Margaret Johnson Patterson Bartlett
lineage.note: Campaigned with her mother to preserve the Greeneville homestead and gave tours there until 1976.

records.today: The family's Greeneville properties are now the Andrew Johnson National Historic Site (monument 1942, NHS 1963), thanks largely to descendants' preservation efforts. Margaret Johnson Patterson Bartlett, who died in 1992, is the last family member buried in its cemetery. 8 August is still marked locally as Emancipation Day, recalling the date Johnson freed the people he enslaved.

records.name: Carroll family (Charles Carroll of Carrollton; Doughoregan Manor)
records.scaleNote: A December 1773 inventory lists 330 enslaved people at Doughoregan Manor alone (Maryland Center for History and Culture); Carroll was among the largest enslavers in Maryland, with further people at Homewood and other estates.
records.origins: Charles Carroll 'the Settler' arrived in 1688 as attorney general for the Catholic proprietor Lord Baltimore and amassed land, lending and an ironworks interest. His grandson Charles Carroll of Carrollton (1737–1832) was the only Catholic signer of the Declaration and reputedly the richest man in the colonies.
records.role_summary: The Carrolls' fortune — tobacco and grain plantations, the Baltimore Iron Works, money-lending and land — rested on hundreds of enslaved people. Carroll of Carrollton wrote in favor of gradual abolition yet held some 300+ people at Doughoregan and others at Homewood (Baltimore), where enslaved gardener Izadod Conner is credited with shaping the grounds.

roleDetail.d: The family-by-family list of 330 enslaved people at Doughoregan is one of Maryland's most detailed plantation records.
At least 36 enslaved people lived and worked at Homewood, built for Carroll's son from 1801.
Carroll's cousin Archbishop John Carroll founded Georgetown (1789), whose Jesuit sponsors also held enslaved people on Maryland plantations.

records.legacy: Carroll County and many Maryland institutions bear the name; Carroll helped launch the B&O Railroad (1828). Homewood Museum at Johns Hopkins and the Maryland Center for History and Culture now research the enslaved families of Doughoregan and Homewood (e.g., the Conner family).

legacyDetail.d: Johns Hopkins' Homewood Museum has projects honoring people enslaved on the estate.
A 2022 Maryland Historical Magazine article examines Carroll and the enslaved families of Doughoregan.

sources.label: Maryland Center for History and Culture — List of negroes on Doohoregan Manor, 1773
The Cultural Landscape Foundation — Izadod Conner
WYPR — Shining a light on enslavers in Congress (Homewood)
The Daily Record — Historic Howard County property will stay untouched (2011)

connections.label: Settler was Lord Baltimore's attorney general

lineage.name: Charles Carroll the Settler
lineage.note: Irish Catholic lawyer sent in 1688 as attorney general for Lord Baltimore; built the land, lending and ironworks base.

lineage.name: Charles Carroll of Annapolis
lineage.note: Expanded the estate and held a share in the Baltimore Iron Works, worked by enslaved people.

lineage.name: Charles Carroll of Carrollton
lineage.note: Signer of the Declaration and one of the largest enslavers in Maryland (c. 300 people at Doughoregan and elsewhere).

lineage.name: Mary Darnall Carroll
lineage.note: Cousin from the Catholic Darnall family; marriage kept land within the Catholic gentry.

lineage.name: John Carroll
lineage.note: First Catholic bishop in the United States and founder of Georgetown (1789).

lineage.name: Mary Carroll Caton
lineage.note: Married Richard Caton; their daughters married into the British aristocracy (Marchioness Wellesley, Duchess of Leeds, Baroness Stafford).

lineage.name: Charles Carroll of Homewood
lineage.note: Received Homewood (Baltimore) from his father; the house is now Homewood Museum at Johns Hopkins.

lineage.name: John Lee Carroll
lineage.note: Governor of Maryland (1876–1880) who lived at Doughoregan Manor.

records.today: Doughoregan Manor is still owned and lived in by Carroll descendants, who are private and not named here. In 2011 Howard County paid $19.1 million to keep about 500 acres from development. Homewood Museum (Johns Hopkins) and the Maryland Center for History and Culture research the families the Carrolls enslaved.

records.name: Lloyd family of Wye House
records.scaleNote: Edward Lloyd IV held 305 enslaved people in 1790 and Edward Lloyd V c. 420 in 1810 (Maryland State Archives); across generations the estate enslaved more than 1,000 people on up to 42,000 acres.
records.origins: Edward Lloyd, a Welsh Puritan, settled on the Wye River in the 1650s. Successive Edward Lloyds became one of Maryland's wealthiest landholding and enslaving dynasties; Edward Lloyd V was governor (1809–1811) and U.S. Senator (1819–1826).
records.role_summary: Wye House was the hub of a dozen outlying farms, each worked by 18–47 enslaved people under overseers, producing grain and tobacco. Frederick Douglass spent part of his childhood there in 1824 (owned by overseer Aaron Anthony) and described its brutality in his 1845 Narrative; later Lloyds moved enslaved people to new cotton plantations in the Deep South.

roleDetail.d: In 1824 c. 181 enslaved people lived at the Wye House home plantation itself, per the Frederick Douglass Papers.
Douglass's Narrative made 'Colonel Lloyd's' plantation emblematic of Chesapeake slavery.
Edward Lloyd VI acquired cotton land in Mississippi, Arkansas and Louisiana and transferred enslaved people there.

records.legacy: Wye House remains privately owned by Lloyd descendants (11th–12th generation), who have allowed University of Maryland archaeologists (from 2005) to excavate the 'Long Green' quarters and greenhouse, where African-derived protective objects were found. Exhibits and a database of hundreds of enslaved people's names have resulted.

legacyDetail.d: UMD's project, conducted with the family's permission and with descendant communities, has documented quarters, greenhouse and named individuals.

sources.label: Maryland State Archives — Aaron Anthony biography (Lloyd holdings, Douglass)
NPR — Plantation Dig Reveals Md. Town's Painful Past
Talbot Spy — UMD Wye House archeology exhibition opens at Academy Art Museum

connections.label: moved enslaved people to Deep South

lineage.name: Edward Lloyd I
lineage.note: Welsh Puritan who settled on the Wye River in the 1650s.

lineage.name: Edward Lloyd IV
lineage.note: 'The Patriot'; built the present Wye House in the 1780s.

lineage.name: Mary Tayloe Lloyd Key
lineage.note: Married Francis Scott Key in 1802, linking the Lloyds to the Keys and Howards.

lineage.name: Edward Lloyd V
lineage.note: Governor and U.S. Senator; at its peak the family enslaved more than 1,000 people across about 42,000 acres.

lineage.name: Aaron Anthony
lineage.note: Lloyd's general manager and the enslaver of the young Frederick Douglass.

lineage.name: Frederick Douglass
lineage.note: Lived at Wye House as a boy and described it in his autobiographies; returned in 1881.

lineage.name: Lloyd descendants
lineage.note: Still own about 1,300 acres; an 11th-generation descendant inherited in 1993 and opened the site to University of Maryland archaeologists in 2005.

records.today: Wye House is still privately owned by Lloyd descendants, now in the 11th–12th generation on the property; they have allowed archaeology but are private and not named here. Descendants of the enslaved community, many living in nearby Unionville, work with University of Maryland researchers, and the finds have been shown at the Academy Art Museum in Easton.

records.name: Ridgely family of Hampton (Towson)
records.scaleNote: The Ridgelys enslaved over 500 people from the colonial era to 1864: c. 130 in 1783, more than 300 by 1790, nearly 350 in 1829, 61 in 1860, per NPS.
records.origins: Charles Ridgely bought 1,500 acres in northern Baltimore County in 1745 and opened the Northampton Ironworks in 1761. His son Captain Charles Ridgely expanded holdings to c. 24,000 acres, partly from confiscated Loyalist land, and built the Hampton mansion (completed 1790).
records.role_summary: Enslaved people — alongside convict and indentured servants — worked the ironworks, quarries, fields and mansion. Governor Charles Carnan Ridgely's 1829 will codicil freed people within set age bands, one of Maryland's largest manumissions, but it split families; his son John bought c. 60 more people and slavery continued at Hampton until Maryland abolished it in 1864.

roleDetail.d: Northampton Ironworks supplied iron, including during the Revolution, using enslaved and bound labor.
Women 25–45 and men 28–45 were freed; younger people waited, and those over 45 were bequeathed to heirs under Maryland law.
Daniel Harris was freed but his three-year-old daughter Mary was not; he bought her freedom in 1831.

records.legacy: Hampton passed to the federal government in 1948 as Hampton National Historic Site. NPS's 2020 study 'Tracing the Lives of the Enslaved' identified hundreds of living descendants of those freed in 1829, and the site interprets its quarters and enslaved community.

legacyDetail.d: The NPS Ethnographic Overview traces families freed in 1829 through generations to today.

sources.label: NPS — Tracing the Lives of the Enslaved study
NPS History — Hampton NHS Maryland Historical Magazine (1948)

lineage.name: Col. Charles Ridgely 'the Merchant'
lineage.note: Baltimore merchant who bought the Northampton tract in 1745.

lineage.name: Capt. Charles Ridgely
lineage.note: Ran the Northampton Ironworks with enslaved and convict labour and built Hampton; childless.

lineage.name: Charles Carnan Ridgely
lineage.note: Born Charles Ridgely Carnan; inherited Hampton on condition he take the Ridgely name (1790). Governor of Maryland; held over 300 enslaved people. His will freed all those under 45.

lineage.name: John Carnan Ridgely and Eliza Ridgely
lineage.note: Inherited the mansion and 4,500 acres and went on enslaving people at Hampton until 1864.

lineage.name: John Ridgely Jr.
lineage.note: Last family owner; the Avalon Foundation (Ailsa Mellon Bruce) bought the mansion and gave it to the U.S. in 1948, and he lived in the farmhouse until his death.

records.today: Hampton has been a National Historic Site since 1948, and the family's last land passed to the Interior Department in 1980. The NPS 'Tracing the Lives of the Enslaved' study (2020) traced living descendants of the people the Ridgelys enslaved. The site does not name living Ridgely descendants.

records.name: Howard family (John Eager Howard; Belvidere)
records.scaleNote: No full count published; Howard's papers record buying, selling and manumitting enslaved people, his 1827 estate sale at Belvidere included enslaved persons, and the 1846 inventory of his son George Howard's estate at Waverly listed 25 enslaved men, women and children.
records.origins: John Eager Howard (1752–1827) inherited Baltimore County land, won fame at the Battle of Cowpens (1781), and served as governor of Maryland (1788–1791) and U.S. Senator. He became one of Baltimore's largest landowners as the city expanded over his estates.
records.role_summary: Howard's wealth was chiefly urban land, but he enslaved people on his Belvidere estate and other properties. His correspondence discusses the purchase and sale of enslaved people and deeds of manumission; his son George Howard, governor 1831–1833, enslaved people at Waverly (Marriottsville).

roleDetail.d: Letters to Virgil Maxcy (NYPL) discuss buying and selling enslaved people and signing manumission deeds.
A sale at 'Belvidere House' after Howard's death included enslaved people, per Maryland Center for History and Culture holdings.
After George Howard's death in August 1846, his estate inventory listed 25 enslaved people at Waverly.

records.legacy: Howard County, Howard and Eager Streets, and a 1904 equestrian statue in Mount Vernon Place honor him; he donated the land for Baltimore's Washington Monument. Public reckoning with his slaveholding has so far been limited.

legacyDetail.d: Mount Vernon Place was laid out on land Howard gave, with his statue in the north garden.

sources.label: NYPL Archives — John Eager Howard letters to Virgil Maxcy

lineage.name: Cornelius Howard and Ruth Eager
lineage.note: The Eager land on which Baltimore later spread came through John Eager Howard's mother.

lineage.name: Margaret 'Peggy' Chew Howard
lineage.note: Daughter of Benjamin Chew of Cliveden, Philadelphia, whose family also held enslaved people in Delaware and Maryland.

lineage.name: George Howard
lineage.note: Governor of Maryland; planter at Waverly (Marriottsville).

lineage.name: Benjamin Chew Howard
lineage.note: Congressman and U.S. Supreme Court Reporter of Decisions (1843–1860), the period that included Dred Scott v. Sandford.

lineage.name: Charles Howard and Francis Key Howard
lineage.note: Charles married Elizabeth Key, daughter of Francis Scott Key; father and son were imprisoned at Fort McHenry in 1861 as Southern sympathisers.

records.today: Belvidere was demolished in the 1870s and the estates became Baltimore's Mount Vernon, Howard and Eager street districts. No publicly documented descendants are named here; the statue and place names are the main legacy.

records.name: Thomas Jefferson
records.scaleNote: Jefferson enslaved more than 600 (over 610) people in his lifetime, per Monticello's Getting Word project; c. 130 people were advertised for sale after his death to pay $107,000 of debt.
records.origins: Jefferson inherited land and enslaved people from his father Peter Jefferson and, through his wife Martha Wayles Skelton, from John Wayles — an inheritance that included Elizabeth Hemings and her children. Wayles had acted as an agent in slave-ship sales in Virginia.
records.role_summary: Author of the Declaration's 'all men are created equal', Jefferson ran Monticello and Poplar Forest with enslaved labor (tobacco, then wheat, a nailery and household work), bought and sold people, and freed only a handful. Most historians accept that he fathered Sally Hemings's children; as president he signed the 1807 Act ending legal imports.

roleDetail.d: Monticello's records identify more than 610 people Jefferson enslaved over his life.
After his death, nearly 100 people were sold over five days at Monticello and at least 33 more in 1829, scattering families.
Monticello and most scholars conclude Jefferson fathered six children with Hemings, whom he enslaved.
He urged and signed the ban on importing captives effective 1 January 1808.

records.legacy: Monticello (Thomas Jefferson Foundation) now centers slavery in its interpretation, including the 2018 'Life of Sally Hemings' exhibit, and its Getting Word Oral History Project (since 1993) has recorded over 200 interviews with descendants. The University of Virginia, which Jefferson founded, has built a Memorial to Enslaved Laborers.

legacyDetail.d: The project documents hundreds of descendants of Monticello's enslaved families.

lineage.name: Peter Jefferson
lineage.note: Surveyor and planter who left Thomas land and enslaved people.

lineage.name: John Wayles
lineage.note: Lawyer, planter and agent for Bristol slave-trading firms; his estate brought Jefferson the Hemings family and about 11,000 acres, along with heavy debts.

lineage.name: Martha Wayles Skelton Jefferson
lineage.note: Wayles's daughter and Sally Hemings's half-sister.

lineage.name: Hemings family
lineage.note: Elizabeth Hemings and her children, including Sally, came to Monticello through Wayles's estate.

lineage.name: Martha Jefferson Randolph
lineage.note: Kept house at Monticello; her children inherited the debts.

lineage.name: Thomas Jefferson Randolph
lineage.note: Ran the 1827 sale of about 130 enslaved people to pay Jefferson's debts.

lineage.name: Uriah P. Levy
lineage.note: Bought Monticello in 1834 after a brief sale to James Barclay; the Thomas Jefferson Foundation bought it from his heirs in 1923.

records.today: Both lines of descendants are public. The Monticello Association is the society of Jefferson's documented white descendants. Hemings descendants such as Shannon Lanier, co-author of 'Jefferson's Children' (2000), have spoken widely about the family. Journalist Lucian K. Truscott IV, a Randolph-line descendant, campaigned for Hemings descendants to be recognised. Monticello's Getting Word project has recorded descendants of the enslaved community since 1993.

today_people.name: Gayle Jessup White
today_people.relation: descendant of Peter Hemings (son of John Wayles and Betty Hemings) and of Jefferson's family, per DNA research in her book
today_people.role: Author of 'Reclamation' (2021); Public Relations & Community Engagement Officer at the Thomas Jefferson Foundation (Monticello), first descendant employed there

source.label: Virginia Museum of History & Culture — Reclamation: How a Monticello descendant uncovered and restored her family's heritage

today_people.name: Lucian K. Truscott IV
today_people.relation: descendant of Thomas Jefferson via the Randolph line
today_people.role: Journalist and author; campaigned for Hemings descendants' admission to the Monticello Association

records.name: Austin Woolfolk
records.scaleNote: Baltimore's leading slave trader of the 1820s–30s, making tens of thousands of dollars a year; part of a Baltimore–New Orleans coastal trade that carried an estimated 15,000–20,000 people 1818–1860.
records.base: Pratt and Cove Streets, Baltimore, Maryland
records.origins: Woolfolk began trading in Baltimore around 1816, aged about 19, buying people in taverns and hotels; his uncle sold people he sent overland to Georgia. He belonged to a family network of traders.
records.role_summary: Woolfolk professionalised the Baltimore trade with a fixed residence and private jail on West Pratt Street, 'CASH FOR NEGROES' advertising and a network of rural agents. He marched coffles south and shipped captives from Fells Point and the Inner Harbor to New Orleans; Frederick Douglass recalled his chained gangs passing at night.

roleDetail.d: His fixed pen model was later copied by Franklin & Armfield, per Baltimore Heritage.

On 9 January 1827 he beat abolitionist editor Benjamin Lundy, who had called him a 'monster in human shape'; he pleaded guilty and Judge Nicholas Brice fined him one dollar plus costs, remarking that the trade was beneficial.
Coastwise ships carried his captives to New Orleans; one, the Decatur (1826), saw a revolt by those aboard.

records.legacy: His Pratt Street site now lies under a divided highway near MLK Boulevard; Baltimore Heritage and city historical markers document it. He retired wealthy in 1842; Joseph Donovan took over the site.

legacyDetail.d: Baltimore Heritage's 'Slave Trade in Baltimore' tour marks Woolfolk's jail.

sources.label: Baltimore Heritage — Site of Austin Woolfolk's Slave Jail
AHA 2018 — Baltimore to New Orleans coastal slave trade (paper abstract)
History News Network — What Else You Should Know About Baltimore

lineage.name: John Woolfolk
lineage.note: Sold the people Austin marched from Baltimore to Georgia and ran the family's New Orleans and Natchez sales agency.

lineage.name: Woolfolk brothers and cousins (incl. Sowell Woolfolk)
lineage.note: Brothers and relatives came to Maryland to buy people and drove coffles overland to Augusta, Georgia.

lineage.name: Benjamin Lundy
lineage.note: Abolitionist editor whom Woolfolk beat in Baltimore in 1827; a court fined Woolfolk only $1.

lineage.name: Frederick Douglass
lineage.note: Named 'Austin Woldfolk' in his 1845 Narrative as the trader who loomed over enslaved Marylanders.

lineage.name: Joseph Donovan
lineage.note: Took over the Pratt Street site after Woolfolk withdrew.

records.today: No publicly documented descendants have been traced; his profits went into land and enslaved people in Louisiana and Georgia. The Pratt Street site is now under highway lanes and is marked by Baltimore Heritage.

records.name: Hope H. Slatter
records.scaleNote: A leading Baltimore trader 1835–late 1840s, shipping captives to New Orleans and holding others in his jail at 25 cents a day; no reliable total is published.
records.base: Pratt Street (between Sharp and Howard), Baltimore, Maryland
records.origins: Born in Georgia, Slatter worked with his brother Shadrack in New Orleans before moving to Baltimore in 1835. His son Henry joined the business.
records.role_summary: From 1838 Slatter ran a private jail on Pratt Street — his house at one end, a two-storey brick prison at the other — buying Chesapeake people under 'Cash for Negroes' adverts, boarding others' captives, and shipping people south by sea. He sold the business to the Campbell brothers in the late 1840s and retired to Mobile.

roleDetail.d: Baltimore Heritage dates the jail at 224 W. Pratt Street to 1838.
1843 Baltimore Sun ads offered to hold people for 25 cents a day.
B. M. and W. L. Campbell continued the trade from the site.

records.legacy: The site, near today's Camden Yards area of Pratt Street, is marked in Baltimore Heritage's slave-trade tour. Slatter died of yellow fever in Mobile in 1853.

legacyDetail.d: Baltimore Heritage documents the 'Slatter/Campbell Slave Jail'.

sources.label: Baltimore Heritage — Site of Slatter/Campbell Slave Jail
Afrolumens Project — Hope H. Slatter, 1843 advertisement
Wikipedia — Bernard M. Campbell and Walter L. Campbell

lineage.name: Shadrack Slatter
lineage.note: Partner in the family's earlier trading in New Orleans and Georgia.

lineage.name: Henry Slatter
lineage.note: Worked in his father's Baltimore business.

lineage.name: Bernard M. and Walter L. Campbell
lineage.note: Bought Slatter's Pratt Street business in 1848, after his purchase of about thirty escapees from the schooner Pearl, and ran 'Slatter's old stand' until the Army freed the jail in 1863.

records.today: No publicly documented descendants have been traced. The pen was torn down in 1864; Baltimore Heritage's slave-trade tour now marks the site near Camden Yards.

records.name: Ball family of South Carolina
records.scaleNote: Between 1698 and 1865 six generations owned more than twenty Cooper River rice plantations and enslaved nearly 4,000 people, per the Ball Family Slaveholder Index; Isaac Ball alone held 571.
records.base: Comingtee, Cooper River, near Charleston, South Carolina
records.origins: Elias Ball arrived from England in 1698 to claim a share of the Comingtee plantation inherited from his uncle John Coming. The family expanded across the Cooper River's tidal rice lands.
records.role_summary: The Balls bought captives directly off transatlantic ships in Charleston — in 1756 Elias Ball bought five children from the Hare, sold by Henry Laurens's firm, including a ten-year-old girl from Sierra Leone he named Priscilla. Enslaved West Africans' rice-growing knowledge and labor made the Lowcountry estates profitable.

roleDetail.d: Laurens's account book records the sale of five children from the Hare to Elias Ball on 30 June 1756.
Over twenty plantations, with surviving records for twenty-eight Ball properties.
Edward Ball linked the Hare to Bunce Island; newer research suggests most captives were bought along the Sierra Leone–Guinea coast.

records.legacy: Descendant Edward Ball's 'Slaves in the Family' (1998, National Book Award) traced both the family and descendants of the people it enslaved. Research by Ball and Joseph Opala connected Thomalind Martin Polite, Priscilla's descendant, to Sierra Leone (homecoming 2005), a story now in the International African American Museum.

legacyDetail.d: Ball's book began after a family reunion where no one mentioned the 4,000 people the family had enslaved.
Yale's Gilder Lehrman Center documented Polite's 2005 visit to Sierra Leone.

sources.label: Lowcountry Africana — Ball Family Slaveholder Index
Edward Ball — Slaves in the Family
Charleston City Paper — Polite: My family's link to West Africa is told in IAAM exhibit

connections.label: Hare voyage linked to Sierra Leone

lineage.name: John Coming and Affra Harleston Coming
lineage.note: Early Carolina settlers whose Comingtee plantation passed to Elias Ball.

lineage.name: Elias 'Red Cap' Ball
lineage.note: Emigrated from Devon in 1698 and became a Cooper River rice planter at Comingtee; married Elizabeth Harleston and later Mary Delamare.

lineage.name: Eleanor Ball Laurens
lineage.note: Married the Charleston slave-trading merchant Henry Laurens.

lineage.name: Later Ball generations
lineage.note: Spread across Comingtee, Limerick, Kensington and other Cooper River plantations; Edward Ball estimates the family enslaved nearly 4,000 people over 167 years.

lineage.name: Edward Ball
lineage.note: Author of 'Slaves in the Family' (1998), which traced the family and descendants of the people it enslaved; later wrote 'Life of a Klansman' (2020).

lineage.name: Thomalind Martin Polite
lineage.note: Descendant of Priscilla, a child enslaved by the Balls; she visited Sierra Leone in 2005 in a homecoming organised by Joseph Opala.

records.today: Ball family plantations were sold off after 1865. The family's best-known public descendant is Edward Ball, whose 1998 book won the National Book Award. Thomalind Martin Polite has spoken publicly about her line, and her family's story is in the International African American Museum. No other living descendants are named.

records.name: Hampton family (Wade Hampton I, II, III)
records.scaleNote: Wade Hampton I 'may have owned as many as 900' enslaved people by 1820 (South Carolina Encyclopedia), and at his 1835 death was said to hold c. 3,000 (a contemporary claim, unverified). In 1860 the Hamptons' Issaquena County, Mississippi, plantations held 335 people per the slave schedules, while Digital History credits Wade Hampton III with c. 900 in the Delta — counts vary by source and date.
records.base: Columbia, South Carolina (Millwood); The Houmas, Louisiana; Mississippi
records.origins: Wade Hampton I (1752–1835), a Revolutionary officer and land speculator, became a cotton planter in the South Carolina midlands and in 1811 bought Louisiana land (The Houmas) that he made the state's largest sugar operation, selling c. $100,000 a year by 1827.
records.role_summary: Three generations built one of the antebellum South's largest slaveholding fortunes in cotton and sugar across South Carolina, Louisiana and Mississippi. Wade Hampton III, a Confederate general, became governor in 1876 after a campaign marked by Red Shirt violence that ended Reconstruction in South Carolina.

roleDetail.d: The Houmas, worked by enslaved people, made Hampton I Louisiana's largest sugar producer by 1827.
Hampton II and III held plantations in South Carolina and the Mississippi Delta (Hampton II's own Walnut Ridge tract was 2,529 acres).
Hampton III's 1876 election, backed by armed Red Shirts, restored white minority rule.

records.legacy: A Wade Hampton III equestrian statue stands on the South Carolina State House grounds, and his name remains on schools and places, some renamed after 2020 debates. Houmas House is a Louisiana museum; Millwood's ruins survive near Columbia.

legacyDetail.d: Hampton monuments and names have been debated as part of Confederate memorial reviews.

sources.label: South Carolina Encyclopedia — Hampton, Wade I
South Carolina Encyclopedia — Hampton, Wade II
Digital History (University of Houston) — Biographical sidebar: Wade Hampton

connections.label: War of 1812 era (Hampton I a U.S. general)

lineage.name: Anthony Hampton
lineage.note: Settler killed in a Cherokee raid on the South Carolina frontier.

lineage.name: Wade Hampton I
lineage.note: Revolutionary officer and speculator; bought The Houmas (Louisiana) in 1811; said at his death to hold about 3,000 enslaved people.

lineage.name: John Smith Preston and Caroline Hampton Preston
lineage.note: Managed The Houmas by 1825 and sold it to John Burnside in 1857.

lineage.name: Wade Hampton II
lineage.note: Ran Millwood near Columbia and Mississippi cotton plantations.

lineage.name: Wade Hampton III
lineage.note: Confederate general and governor (1876), carried into office by the Red Shirt campaign of terror; later U.S. Senator.

records.today: Millwood was burned in 1865 and survives only as ruins; Houmas House is a privately owned museum and garden. Wade Hampton III's State House statue remains, though some Hampton-named places were renamed after 2020. No publicly documented living descendants are named here.

records.name: Middleton family of South Carolina
records.scaleNote: The Middleton Place Foundation identifies some 2,800 people enslaved by the Middleton family between 1738 and 1865 across their rice plantations.
records.base: Middleton Place, Ashley River, South Carolina
records.origins: The Middletons arrived in Carolina from Barbados in the late 1600s. Henry Middleton acquired the Ashley River estate by marriage in 1741 and later presided over the First Continental Congress; his son Arthur signed the Declaration of Independence.
records.role_summary: Enslaved Africans and their descendants built and worked the Middletons' rice fields, terraced gardens and house; the family's wealth and political leadership — from Congress to the 1860 Ordinance of Secession, which Williams Middleton signed — rested on their labor.

roleDetail.d: The Ashley River rice fields were likely built by enslaved people brought from West Africa.
Williams Middleton signed South Carolina's Ordinance of Secession (1860); Union troops burned the house in 1865.

records.legacy: Middleton Place (Foundation-owned, a National Historic Landmark) runs the 'Beyond the Fields' exhibit and tours on its enslaved people, and since 2006 has hosted joint reunions of Black and white Middleton descendants (c. 300 attended in 2016), which led to a tuition assistance program.

legacyDetail.d: Begun in 2006 at the suggestion of an African American descendant.
A freedmen's dwelling on site interprets enslaved and post-emancipation lives.

sources.label: Suffolk University — Reinterpreting Life on a Southern Plantation
The Cultural Landscape Foundation — Middleton Place
Post and Courier — Charles Duell wins award for historic preservation efforts
Charleston Magazine — Charles Duell steps down after nearly 50 years

lineage.name: Arthur Middleton (1681–1737)
lineage.note: Led the 1719 revolt against the Lords Proprietors; acting governor.

lineage.name: Charles H. P. Duell

records.today: Middleton Place belongs to the Middleton Place Foundation, set up by descendant Charles H. P. Duell, who led it for decades before stepping back around 2018. Since 2006 it has held joint reunions of white Middleton descendants and descendants of the people the family enslaved. Private family members are not named.

records.name: Pinckney family of South Carolina
records.scaleNote: Charles Cotesworth Pinckney enslaved c. 250 people, per NPS; Charles Pinckney's Snee Farm (715 acres) and other estates were worked by enslaved people producing rice and indigo.
records.base: Charleston and Snee Farm, Mount Pleasant, South Carolina
records.origins: Eliza Lucas Pinckney developed indigo as a South Carolina export crop in the 1740s using enslaved labor and expertise. Her sons Charles Cotesworth and Thomas Pinckney and their cousin Charles Pinckney became leading Federalist-era statesmen.
records.role_summary: At the 1787 Constitutional Convention C. C. Pinckney and Charles Pinckney insisted South Carolina would reject a Constitution that empowered Congress to ban the Atlantic slave trade, helping secure the clause protecting imports until 1808.

roleDetail.d: NPS's convention chronicle records C. C. Pinckney's 22 August 1787 argument for protecting slave imports.
Charles Pinckney inherited Snee Farm in 1782 and grew rice and indigo with enslaved workers; a 1787 inventory lists them by name.

records.legacy: Charles Pinckney National Historic Site (est. 1988) preserves 28 acres of Snee Farm and uses archaeology to interpret the enslaved community there.

legacyDetail.d: The park's 'Enslaved Community of Snee Farm' presents archaeology of quarters and daily life.

sources.label: NPS — Enslaved Community of Snee Farm

connections.label: C. C. Pinckney served in Washington administration

lineage.name: George Lucas
lineage.note: Antigua planter and officer who left his teenage daughter to manage his South Carolina plantations.

lineage.name: Eliza Lucas Pinckney
lineage.note: Developed indigo as an export crop with enslaved workers' skills; married Charles Pinckney in 1744.

lineage.name: Charles Pinckney (c. 1699–1758)
lineage.note: Chief justice of South Carolina.

lineage.name: Charles Cotesworth Pinckney and Thomas Pinckney
lineage.note: Federalist statesmen who defended slavery and the slave trade at the 1787 Convention.

lineage.name: Charles Pinckney (1757–1824)
lineage.note: Framer and owner of Snee Farm; married Mary Eleanor Laurens, daughter of Henry Laurens.

lineage.name: Henry Laurens Pinckney
lineage.note: Congressman and Charleston mayor, author of the 1836 House 'gag rule' resolutions against antislavery petitions.

records.today: Snee Farm is the Charles Pinckney National Historic Site, which interprets its enslaved community through archaeology. No publicly documented living descendants are named here; the family's plantations were broken up after 1865.

records.name: Port of Baltimore (Fells Point and Inner Harbor)
records.description: Baltimore grew as an export port for Chesapeake tobacco and grain produced largely by enslaved people, and became a hub of the domestic slave trade: slave jails clustered between the Inner Harbor and Fells Point, and an estimated 15,000–20,000 people were shipped by sea to New Orleans between 1818 and 1860 (AHA 2018 paper; NARA M1895 manifests). Baltimore also had the largest free Black population of any U.S. city by 1860.

records.name: Pratt Street slave jails, Baltimore
records.description: Private jails on West Pratt Street held people bought in the Chesapeake before sale south: Austin Woolfolk's at Pratt and Cove (by 1821), Hope H. Slatter's at 224 W. Pratt (1838, later the Campbells'), and Joseph Donovan's. Sites are marked by Baltimore Heritage; most lie under modern roads near Camden Yards and MLK Boulevard.

records.name: Mount Vernon
records.description: George Washington's 8,000-acre, five-farm plantation on the Potomac, where 317 enslaved people lived in 1799. Owned since 1858 by the Mount Vernon Ladies' Association, it now interprets slavery extensively, including the 1983 Slave Memorial and ongoing burial-ground archaeology.

records.name: Monticello
records.description: Thomas Jefferson's Albemarle County plantation, where hundreds of enslaved people worked fields, a nailery and the household. Most of the enslaved community was sold in 1827 to pay his debts; today the Thomas Jefferson Foundation interprets Mulberry Row, Sally Hemings's life and descendant histories through Getting Word.

records.name: The Hermitage (Nashville)
records.description: Andrew Jackson's cotton plantation, where about 150 people were enslaved at his death in 1845. The Andrew Jackson Foundation located its enslaved cemetery (at least 28 burials) in 2024 and is forming a descendant advisory committee.

records.name: Riversdale (Riverdale Park, Maryland)
records.description: Plantation house completed by Rosalie Stier Calvert and George Calvert in the early 1800s, worked by enslaved people including diarist Adam Francis Plummer; part of its land became the University of Maryland campus. Now a National Historic Landmark house museum run by M-NCPPC that interprets its enslaved workforce.

records.name: Wye House
records.description: Seat of the Lloyd family on Maryland's Eastern Shore since the 1650s, hub of farms that enslaved hundreds; Frederick Douglass lived there as an enslaved child in 1824. Still privately owned by Lloyd descendants; UMD archaeology since 2005 has uncovered quarters and African-derived ritual objects.

records.name: Hampton National Historic Site (Towson)
records.description: The Ridgely family's Baltimore County plantation and ironworks estate, with a mansion completed in 1790 and surviving stone slave quarters; nearly 350 people were enslaved there in 1829. NPS has operated it since 1948 and researches descendants of the enslaved.

records.name: Doughoregan Manor
records.description: The Carroll family's c. 10,000-acre Howard County estate, where a 1773 inventory listed 330 enslaved people by family. It remained in Carroll family hands long after Charles Carroll of Carrollton's death in 1832 and is a National Historic Landmark.

records.name: Catoctin Furnace
records.description: Iron furnace founded in 1776 by Thomas Johnson and three of his brothers in Frederick County and worked by enslaved African American ironworkers; it made iron for the Continental Army. Its African American cemetery (c. 100 graves; donated to Cunningham Falls State Park in 2026) is the subject of a 2023 Science ancient-DNA study linking nearly 42,000 living people to 27 individuals buried there.

records.name: Maryland Act of 1664 (lifelong slavery)
records.description: Act of the Maryland assembly, under the Calverts' proprietary government, declaring that enslaved Africans in the province and those imported later would serve 'durante vita' (for life), with their children enslaved as well. It gave legislative sanction to slavery practiced since the 1640s and anchored the Chesapeake tobacco economy.

records.name: Maryland Constitution of 1864 (abolition)
records.description: Maryland's third constitution, ratified narrowly by referendum on 12–13 October 1864 (soldiers' votes provided the margin) and effective 1 November 1864, abolished slavery in the state a year before the 13th Amendment. 1 November is now marked as Maryland Emancipation Day.

events.title: Maryland makes slavery lifelong
events.text: Under the Calvert proprietorship, Maryland's assembly declared that enslaved Africans would serve 'durante vita' and their children would be enslaved.

source.label: Maryland State Archives — Blacks Before the Law in Colonial Maryland

events.title: Elias Ball buys 'Priscilla' off the Hare
events.text: Henry Laurens's firm sold five children from the Sierra Leone voyage of the Hare to Elias Ball, including a ten-year-old girl he named Priscilla.

events.title: Washington sells Tom to St. Kitts
events.text: George Washington shipped Tom, a Mount Vernon foreman, to the Caribbean for sale, receiving rum, sweetmeats and coin in return.

events.title: Mount Vernon census: 317 people
events.text: Washington's census listed 317 enslaved people — 123 his own, 153 Custis dower people and c. 40 rented; his will freed his own after Martha's death (1801).

source.label: Mount Vernon — Census of the Enslaved Population

events.title: Import ban leaves domestic trade open
events.text: Jefferson signed, and Speaker Nathaniel Macon's House passed, the ban on importing captives from 1808 — after which Chesapeake enslavers increasingly sold people south.

events.title: Jackson drives a coffle on the Natchez Trace
events.text: Andrew Jackson confronted federal agent Silas Dinsmoor, who demanded passes for the enslaved people Jackson was taking south to market.

source.label: Scalawag — Ending the myth of the historic Natchez Trace

events.title: Monticello dispersal sale
events.text: To pay Jefferson's debts, nearly 100 enslaved people were auctioned at Monticello over five days in January, splitting families.

events.title: Ridgely will frees Hampton people by age
events.text: Gov. Charles Carnan Ridgely's codicil manumitted adults in set age bands — one of Maryland's largest manumissions — while leaving others enslaved.

events.title: Maryland Jesuits sell 272+ people
events.text: Jesuits sold at least 272 people from southern Maryland plantations to Louisiana for $115,000 to relieve Georgetown College's debts.

source.label: Georgetown Slavery Archive — Sale of Maryland Jesuit enslaved community, 1838

events.title: Maryland abolishes slavery
events.text: Maryland's new constitution, narrowly ratified by referendum, ended slavery in the state on 1 November 1864.

source.label: Maryland State Archives — Constitutional Convention of 1864

events.title: 'Slaves in the Family' wins National Book Award
events.text: Edward Ball's history of his family's rice plantations and the c. 4,000 people they enslaved won the National Book Award for nonfiction.

source.label: Edward Ball — Slaves in the Family

events.title: Hermitage locates enslaved cemetery; UMD reports on Calvert
events.text: The Hermitage announced it had found the burial ground of people Jackson enslaved, and UMD's 1856 Project documented Charles B. Calvert's enslavement of 52 people.

source.label: AP (via News4Jax) — Hermitage burial site found
